name: Middle cerebral artery superior division infarction
presentation: Weakness and numbness of the face and arm develop suddenly, with the leg relatively spared, and the eyes are turned toward the side of the infarct for the first day or two. In the dominant hemisphere the patient understands but cannot produce fluent speech: output is effortful and telegraphic, repetition is poor and there is often apraxia of the non-paralyzed hand. There is no hemianopia. The picture is a brachiofacial hemiparesis with Broca aphasia.

deficits.distribution: face and arm more than leg
deficits.sign: Brachiofacial hemiparesis with forehead-sparing facial weakness
Transient gaze preference toward the lesion

reasoning: The superior division leaves the middle cerebral trunk in the Sylvian fissure and supplies the frontal and anterior parietal convexity: the lateral part of the precentral and postcentral gyri, the frontal operculum and the frontal eye field. The motor and sensory homunculi place the face and hand on this lateral surface and the leg on the medial surface served by the anterior cerebral artery, so the deficit is brachiofacial. Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers cross in the brainstem, and the face area projects mainly to the contralateral lower facial subnucleus, so the weakness is contralateral and spares the forehead. Broca's area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus lies in the territory, but Wernicke's area in the posterior temporal lobe belongs to the inferior division, which is why comprehension is preserved. The optic radiation runs through the temporal and parietal lobes below the territory, so vision is spared, a useful distinction from a stem occlusion.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the frontal operculum, precentral and postcentral gyri on the lateral convexity, sparing the temporal lobe and deep nuclei.
Cut-off of the superior M2 trunk with preserved inferior trunk flow.

mimics.name: Lacunar pure motor stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Face, arm and leg equally weak, no aphasia or sensory loss

mimics.name: Inferior division infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fluent aphasia and visual field loss without much weakness

mimics.name: Cortical vein thrombosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Seizures, headache and a hemorrhagic cortical lesion on imaging

management: Acute stroke treatment; M2 thrombectomy is considered case by case
Speech and language therapy begun early
Secondary prevention directed at the embolic source
